Lecture 10

Peter–Weyl and completeness

What this lecture does

Lecture 5 proved that matrix coefficients of inequivalent irreducible representations are orthogonal. This lecture proves that finite-dimensional matrix coefficients span a dense subspace of the square-integrable functions on a compact Lie group. It then deduces that every compact Lie group is a closed subgroup of a unitary group.

Two results from earlier courses are special cases of the theorem of this lecture. For a finite group GGG, the regular module gives C[G]≅⨁UEnd⁡(U)\C[G]\cong\bigoplus_U\End(U)C[G]≅⨁U​End(U), so that ∑U(dim⁡U)2=∣G∣\sum_U(\dim U)^2=|G|∑U​(dimU)2=∣G∣ (Finite Groups). For the circle U⁡(1)\UU(1)U(1), a square-integrable function has a Fourier series in the functions einθe^{in\theta}einθ. The Peter–Weyl theorem contains both. Each irreducible representation Π\PiΠ of a compact Lie group KKK gives a block of dΠ2d_\Pi^2dΠ2​ matrix coefficients, and the span of these blocks is dense in L2(K)L^2(K)L2(K). For SU⁡(2)\SU(2)SU(2) the blocks have 1,4,9,…1,4,9,\dots1,4,9,… functions. Compared with a finite group, the new difficulty is the infinite sum.

The proof has three parts. First we average a rank-one projection over the group. The result commutes with the group, and it is a compact operator. Next, its eigenspaces for nonzero eigenvalues are finite-dimensional and invariant, so every unitary representation contains finite-dimensional pieces. Finally we apply this to L2(K)L^2(K)L2(K), where a finite-dimensional invariant piece turns out to consist of matrix coefficients.

10.1 Analytic preliminaries

Throughout, KKK is a compact Lie group. We write ∫Kf(g) dg\int_K f(g)\,dg∫K​f(g)dg for its normalised Haar integral on C(K)C(K)C(K). We import four facts from Lecture 5.

  1. The integral is left and right invariant. It is invariant under g↦g−1g\mapsto g^{-1}g↦g−1, and ∫K1 dg=1\int_K 1\,dg=1∫K​1dg=1.

  2. If f∈C(K)f\in C(K)f∈C(K) is nonnegative and not identically zero, then ∫Kf dg>0\int_K f\,dg>0∫K​fdg>0.

  3. A finite-dimensional continuous representation has an invariant inner product. It is then an orthogonal sum of irreducible subrepresentations.

  4. Schur orthogonality, in the form (10.1) below.

We also import Fubini’s theorem for continuous functions on K×KK\times KK×K from Bröcker–tom Dieck, Section I.5. It states that the two iterated Haar integrals agree.

A bounded operator on a Hilbert space HHH is compact if it is an operator-norm limit of finite-rank operators. A self-adjoint operator TTT on HHH is positive if ⟨v,Tv⟩≥0\langle v,Tv\rangle\ge 0⟨v,Tv⟩≥0 for all v∈Hv\in Hv∈H.

We import the spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators from Linear Algebra for Physics, Weeks 13–14, in the following form. If TTT is compact and self-adjoint, then H=ker⁡T  ⊕^  ⨁^μ≠0ker⁡(T−μ).H=\ker T\;\widehat{\oplus}\;\widehat{\bigoplus}_{\mu\neq 0}\ker(T-\mu).H=kerT⊕​⨁​μ=0​ker(T−μ). Moreover, each ker⁡(T−μ)\ker(T-\mu)ker(T−μ) with μ≠0\mu\ne0μ=0 is finite-dimensional. If T≠0T\neq 0T=0, then TTT has a nonzero eigenvalue.

Definition 10.2. The space L2(K)L^2(K)L2(K) is the Hilbert completion of C(K)C(K)C(K) for the sesquilinear form ⟨f,h⟩=∫Kf(g)‾ h(g) dg\langle f,h\rangle=\int_K\overline{f(g)}\,h(g)\,dg⟨f,h⟩=∫K​f(g)​h(g)dg.

By positivity (H2), this sesquilinear form is an inner product on C(K)C(K)C(K). Hence the map C(K)→L2(K)C(K)\to L^2(K)C(K)→L2(K) is injective. An element of L2(K)L^2(K)L2(K) is continuous if it lies in C(K)C(K)C(K). Only continuous elements have values f(x)f(x)f(x). For continuous functions, ∥f∥2≤∥f∥∞=sup⁡x∣f(x)∣\|f\|_2\le\|f\|_\infty=\sup_x|f(x)|∥f∥2​≤∥f∥∞​=supx​∣f(x)∣.

Definition 10.3. A strongly continuous unitary representation of KKK on a Hilbert space HHH is a homomorphism Π\PiΠ from KKK to the unitary group of HHH such that g↦Π(g)vg\mapsto\Pi(g)vg↦Π(g)v is continuous for every v∈Hv\in Hv∈H.

We do not ask for continuity in operator norm. Already right translation on L2(U⁡(1))L^2(\UU(1))L2(U(1)) is not norm continuous (Exercise 10.2).

10.2 An averaged compact operator

Theorem 10.5. Let Π\PiΠ be a strongly continuous unitary representation of KKK on H≠0H\neq0H=0.

  1. The space HHH contains a nonzero finite-dimensional invariant subspace.

  2. The sum HfinH_{\mathrm{fin}}Hfin​ of all finite-dimensional invariant subspaces is dense in HHH.

We look for a nonzero compact self-adjoint intertwiner. An intertwiner has invariant eigenspaces. A compact self-adjoint operator has finite-dimensional eigenspaces for nonzero eigenvalues. Averaging a rank-one projection over KKK gives an intertwiner, and compactness of KKK keeps it a compact operator.

Corollary 10.6. Let Π\PiΠ be a strongly continuous unitary representation of KKK on HHH. Suppose that Π\PiΠ is irreducible, meaning that H≠0H\neq0H=0 and that the only closed invariant subspaces are 000 and HHH. Then dim⁡H<∞\dim H<\inftydimH<∞.

Proof. Since H≠0H\neq0H=0, the existence statement, part (a) of Theorem 10.5, gives a nonzero finite-dimensional invariant subspace WWW. Finite-dimensional subspaces are closed, so W=HW=HW=H by irreducibility. 

This corollary uses compactness. A noncompact Lie group can have irreducible unitary representations of infinite dimension, and Part II treats them.

Proof. The constant 111 is a coefficient of the trivial representation. Conjugates are coefficients, since cu,vΠ‾=cuˉ,vˉΠ‾\overline{c^\Pi_{u,v}}=c^{\overline\Pi}_{\bar u,\bar v}cu,vΠ​​=cuˉ,vˉΠ​ for the inner product on V‾Π\overline V_\PiVΠ​ fixed above. Hence R(K)\Rcoeff(K)R(K) is a subalgebra of C(K)C(K)C(K) that contains the constants and is closed under conjugation. It remains to prove that R(K)\Rcoeff(K)R(K) separates points.

Let x≠yx\ne yx=y and suppose f(x)=f(y)f(x)=f(y)f(x)=f(y) for all f∈R(K)f\in\Rcoeff(K)f∈R(K). Since Lgcu,vΠ=cΠ(g)u,vΠL_gc^\Pi_{u,v}=c^\Pi_{\Pi(g)u,v}Lg​cu,vΠ​=cΠ(g)u,vΠ​, the space R(K)\Rcoeff(K)R(K) is LLL-invariant, so f(g−1x)=f(g−1y)f(g^{-1}x)=f(g^{-1}y)f(g−1x)=f(g−1y) for all ggg. Put s=x−1y≠es=x^{-1}y\ne es=x−1y=e and g=xt−1g=xt^{-1}g=xt−1. Then f(t)=f(ts)f(t)=f(ts)f(t)=f(ts) for all ttt. Hence Rsf=fR_sf=fRs​f=f on R(K)\Rcoeff(K)R(K). Since R(K)\Rcoeff(K)R(K) is dense in L2(K)L^2(K)L2(K) by Proposition 10.10(b), and RsR_sRs​ is bounded, Rs=1R_s=1Rs​=1 on L2(K)L^2(K)L2(K).

Since KKK is Hausdorff, some open U∋eU\ni eU∋e omits sss. By Lemma 10.7(b), some continuous φ≥0\varphi\ge0φ≥0 vanishes outside UUU and satisfies φ(e)>0=φ(s)\varphi(e)>0=\varphi(s)φ(e)>0=φ(s). Then (Rsφ)(e)=φ(s)≠φ(e)(R_s\varphi)(e)=\varphi(s)\neq\varphi(e)(Rs​φ)(e)=φ(s)=φ(e), so Rsφ≠φR_s\varphi\neq\varphiRs​φ=φ in C(K)C(K)C(K). Since C(K)→L2(K)C(K)\to L^2(K)C(K)→L2(K) is injective, Rsφ≠φR_s\varphi\neq\varphiRs​φ=φ in L2(K)L^2(K)L2(K), which contradicts Rs=1R_s=1Rs​=1. Hence R(K)\Rcoeff(K)R(K) separates points.

We import the complex Stone–Weierstrass theorem. For compact Hausdorff XXX, it states that a subalgebra of C(X)C(X)C(X) is uniformly dense if it contains the constants, is closed under conjugation and separates points. We apply it to R(K)⊂C(K)\Rcoeff(K)\subset C(K)R(K)⊂C(K). 

Separation of points has a structural consequence. A compact Lie group is defined abstractly, but it is always a group of matrices.

Theorem 10.13 (Faithful representation). A compact Lie group KKK has an injective finite-dimensional continuous unitary representation σ ⁣:K→U⁡(n)\sigma\colon K\to\UU(n)σ:K→U(n). Its image is a closed subgroup of U⁡(n)\UU(n)U(n), and σ\sigmaσ is an isomorphism of Lie groups from KKK onto this image.

Proof. We add summands to a representation until its kernel is trivial, and we show that this process stops.

Step 1: a smaller kernel. Let (σ,V)(\sigma,V)(σ,V) be a finite-dimensional continuous unitary representation with kernel NNN. For example, the trivial representation on C\CC has kernel KKK. The kernel NNN is a closed subgroup of KKK, so it is a compact Lie group by the closed-subgroup theorem of Lecture 3. Suppose N≠{e}N\ne\{e\}N={e}, and choose s∈Ns\in Ns∈N with s≠es\ne es=e. By the proof of Theorem 10.12, the functions in R(K)\Rcoeff(K)R(K) separate eee and sss. These functions are spanned by matrix coefficients. So some finite-dimensional continuous unitary representation Π\PiΠ has a matrix coefficient with cu,vΠ(s)≠cu,vΠ(e)c^\Pi_{u,v}(s)\ne c^\Pi_{u,v}(e)cu,vΠ​(s)=cu,vΠ​(e). Hence Π(s)≠I\Pi(s)\ne IΠ(s)=I. The direct sum σ⊕Π\sigma\oplus\Piσ⊕Π has kernel N′=N∩ker⁡ΠN'=N\cap\ker\PiN′=N∩kerΠ. This is a closed subgroup of NNN, and N′≠NN'\ne NN′=N because s∉N′s\notin N's∈/N′.

Step 2: comparing N′N'N′ with NNN. Since N′⊆NN'\subseteq NN′⊆N, we have dim⁡N′≤dim⁡N\dim N'\le\dim NdimN′≤dimN. Suppose dim⁡N′=dim⁡N\dim N'=\dim NdimN′=dimN. The inclusion N′→NN'\to NN′→N is an injective immersion between manifolds of equal dimension, so it is a local diffeomorphism. Hence N′N'N′ is open in NNN. Let N0N_0N0​ be the identity component of NNN. Then N′∩N0N'\cap N_0N′∩N0​ is an open subgroup of the connected group N0N_0N0​. An open subgroup is also closed, since its complement is a union of its cosets. So N′∩N0=N0N'\cap N_0=N_0N′∩N0​=N0​, that is, N0⊆N′N_0\subseteq N'N0​⊆N′. The connected set N0N_0N0​ is the largest connected subset of NNN containing eee, so it is also the identity component of N′N'N′.

The components of NNN are the cosets of N0N_0N0​. They are open and they cover the compact group NNN, so there are finitely many. Since N0⊆N′N_0\subseteq N'N0​⊆N′ and N′≠NN'\ne NN′=N, the group N′N'N′ consists of fewer of these cosets. So N′N'N′ has fewer components than NNN.

Step 3: the process stops. By Step 2, each application of Step 1 either lowers the dimension of the kernel, or keeps the dimension and lowers the finite number of components. The dimension can decrease only finitely often. Between two decreases, the number of components decreases at each step. So after finitely many steps the kernel is {e}\{e\}{e}.

Step 4: the image. We now have an injective representation, and an orthonormal basis of its space gives σ ⁣:K→U⁡(n)\sigma\colon K\to\UU(n)σ:K→U(n). The image σ(K)\sigma(K)σ(K) is compact, so it is closed in U⁡(n)\UU(n)U(n), and it is a Lie group by the closed-subgroup theorem. A continuous bijection from a compact space onto a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism. So σ\sigmaσ and its inverse are continuous homomorphisms between Lie groups. By the automatic smoothness theorem of Lecture 3, both are smooth. 

The proof applies to disconnected KKK. Step 3 uses that KKK is a Lie group. Compactness is also needed, since a covering group of a matrix group need not be a matrix group (Lecture 4).

Self-checks

1. Why is the operator (10.2) nonzero, although no invariant vector is known?

Answer. By the definition (10.2), ⟨u,Tu⟩=∫∣⟨Π(g)u,u⟩∣2 dg\langle u,Tu\rangle=\int|\langle\Pi(g)u,u\rangle|^2\,dg⟨u,Tu⟩=∫∣⟨Π(g)u,u⟩∣2dg. The integrand is continuous, nonnegative and equal to 111 at eee. By positivity (H2), the integral is positive. Hence TTT is nonzero.

2. Give dim⁡E2⊂L2(SU⁡(2))\dim E_2\subset L^2(\SU(2))dimE2​⊂L2(SU(2)) and the multiplicity of V2V_2V2​ under RRR.

Answer. The block has dimension dim⁡E2=9\dim E_2=9dimE2​=9. The representation V2V_2V2​ occurs 333 times. Under LLL, E2≅V‾2⊕3E_2\cong\overline{V}_2^{\oplus3}E2​≅V2⊕3​.

3. Why does the coefficient proposition, Proposition 10.10, prove continuity before evaluating at eee?

Answer. Only continuous elements of L2(K)L^2(K)L2(K) have values. Evaluation is not even bounded on R(U⁡(1))\Rcoeff(\UU(1))R(U(1)). For example, the function fN=(2N+1)−1/2∑∣n∣≤Nχnf_N=(2N+1)^{-1/2}\sum_{|n|\le N}\chi_nfN​=(2N+1)−1/2∑∣n∣≤N​χn​ has ∥fN∥2=1\|f_N\|_2=1∥fN​∥2​=1 and fN(1)=2N+1f_N(1)=\sqrt{2N+1}fN​(1)=2N+1​.

Summary

Let KKK be a compact Lie group. In a strongly continuous unitary representation of KKK on H≠0H\neq0H=0, an averaged rank-one projection is a nonzero positive compact intertwiner. Its eigenspaces for nonzero eigenvalues are finite-dimensional and invariant. The finite-dimensional invariant subspaces span a dense subspace. In L2(K)L^2(K)L2(K), smoothing identifies the finite-dimensional RRR-invariant subspaces with spaces of matrix coefficients. Schur orthogonality then gives the Peter–Weyl theorem. Under RRR, and also under LLL, each Π∈Irr⁡(K)\Pi\in\Irr(K)Π∈Irr(K) occurs in L2(K)L^2(K)L2(K) with multiplicity dΠd_\PidΠ​. Density in L2(K)L^2(K)L2(K) shows that R(K)\Rcoeff(K)R(K) separates points. By the Stone–Weierstrass theorem, R(K)\Rcoeff(K)R(K) is therefore uniformly dense in C(K)C(K)C(K). Adding finitely many representations that separate points gives a faithful finite-dimensional unitary representation, so KKK is isomorphic as a Lie group to a closed subgroup of some U⁡(n)\UU(n)U(n).
